analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $20 and makes drugmakers publish their real net prices.
analysis.headline: The insulin price-cap bill drew a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor but never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin through private or employer insurance at $20 per prescription — and $0 for those in high-deductible plans — regardless of their deductible. It would also require insulin makers to publicly publish their net prices (what the drugs actually sell for after rebates and discounts) each quarter, and require pharmacies to sell insulin to uninsured people at that net price plus a capped dispensing charge.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who use insulin would gain the most: anyone on private or employer insurance could get insulin for at most $20 per prescription, with the deductible waived, and those in high-deductible health plans would pay nothing [S2] [S3]. Uninsured people with diabetes would pay the manufacturers' net price (what the drug actually sells for after rebates and discounts) plus capped dispensing fees, instead of the higher list price [S2] [S3]. All insulin users would also benefit from quarterly public disclosure of net prices, a number that today is generally hidden in private deals between manufacturers and middlemen [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with diabetes who use insulin

how_it_helps.text: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs for insured diabetics at $20 per prescription, or $0 for those in high-deductible health plans, by requiring the plan to charge the least of the formula price, the plan's normal coinsurance, or $20.
Waives the deductible for insulin, so patients would no longer pay full price at the pharmacy until their deductible is met — a common reason people ration insulin.
Requires insulin manufacturers to publish the average net price of each insulin drug every quarter, with federal health programs barred from paying any manufacturer that does not comply.
Extends a discounted price to uninsured people with diabetes: pharmacies must sell them insulin at the net price plus dispensing charges capped at 10% of net price, instead of the higher list price.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would bear the largest cost: they would have to publish their net prices each quarter, and federal health programs could not pay for any insulin made by a manufacturer that refused [S3]. Health insurers and employer plans would cover the difference between what patients pay (at most $20, or nothing in high-deductible plans) and the drug's cost, and would have to report any distribution and dispensing charges to the HHS Inspector General [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay but does nothing to lower the underlying price of insulin, so insurers and employers would absorb the difference and the cost could resurface in premiums.
Uninsured people get a weaker deal: they pay the full net price plus up to 10% in dispensing charges, with no $20 cap, so the people least able to afford insulin benefit least.
The only enforcement mechanism against non-compliant manufacturers is a ban on federal health programs paying for their insulin, leaving no clear recourse for privately insured or uninsured patients.
An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill covered only insulin, leaving other high-priced prescription drugs untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: insulin rationing among people with diabetes is a well-documented danger, and a $20 cap with the deductible waived would directly remove the cost barrier for insured patients, while net-price transparency would tackle the hidden rebate system that keeps drug prices high. The costs fall on insulin makers, insurers, and employers rather than taxpayers, though shifting the burden to insurers means some of it could return to patients through premiums. The design is narrower than ideal — no $20 cap for the uninsured and weak enforcement — but on balance it is a straightforward consumer-protection bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2021, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee on the same day.
On July 30, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed.
No hearing, mark-up, vote, or floor action ever followed; the last action in its history is the subcommittee referral.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with a single Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers, health insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers came out ahead, because insulin prices and patient cost-sharing remained unchanged for the rest of the Congress. People with diabetes who struggled with insulin costs gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers and insurers, as before

for.name: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the House.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only named backers were a Republican sponsor and its single Democratic cosponsor, so its support never split along party lines in any measurable way.

industries.note: The bill would force insulin makers to publish net prices quarterly and cut off federal payments to any manufacturer that refused. Because net prices after rebates are typically far below list prices, this disclosure would expose and could compress a long-opaque revenue structure.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Insurers and employer plans would have to absorb most insulin costs once patients' payments were capped at $20 or $0, and would face new reporting requirements on dispensing charges. Their drug pricing is built on the current rebate structure the bill would make public.
The bill defines net price to include all rebates and concessions flowing to PBMs under their contracts, so quarterly publication would strip away the secrecy that PBM rebates depend on.

Pharmacies would have to sell insulin to uninsured people at the published net price plus at most a 10% distribution and dispensing charge, limiting markup on cash sales while providing a clear pricing formula.
